source.title: Understanding Double Descent Requires a Fine-Grained Bias-Variance Decomposition

record.tranche_reason: It analytically studies test error and variance around the interpolation boundary in random-feature kernel regression, a different method and model setting from the original deep-network experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper reports theoretical risk and variance results for random-feature kernel regression, plus test-error curves for ensemble and bagging settings. It also reports NTK variance-component behavior; that result is recorded under fits_no_version because the plotted components do not by themselves establish the total test-error curve. No results on epochs or increasing sample size near the interpolation threshold are reported.
record.test_reason: The paper derives exact asymptotic test loss for random-feature kernel regression across the interpolation threshold. It shows the loss diverges there, pins the divergence on the sampling-initialization interaction variance, and shows label noise is not necessary. That bears on V4 (a non-deep model class) and on V6 (noise/variance dependence). It is not an original source.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. Bias decreases monotonically and is finite at interpolation. The divergence comes from the sampling-initialization interaction terms VPX and VPXε, and appears even without label noise, which only exacerbates it. Bagging or ensembling can reduce or eliminate it.
record.recipe_differences: The study gives an asymptotic theoretical analysis of random-feature kernel regression and its NTK extension, rather than reproducing the original deep-network experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The interpolation behavior changes with averaging over initial parameters or training samples. The NTK supplement also reports nonmonotonic variance-component behavior at a parameter scale distinct from the interpolation threshold.

fits_no_version.finding: For the centered NTK, the variance terms VP, VPX and VPXε are nonmonotonic and peak slightly before n1=m, far past the interpolation threshold. None of them diverge (Fig. S2, Sec. S2.4).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Kernel models can show a second, non-divergent variance bump at a scale distinct from the interpolation threshold.

record.problems: The main results are asymptotic theoretical predictions. The plotted finite-size simulations are described without numerical uncertainty estimates. The test-error curves in Figure 2 are figure-only, and the study does not test epochs or sample-size increases near the threshold.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted for the 60-row limit. NTK variance-component results are recorded as R18 under fits_no_version, not as a test-error row.

untested.parts: No deep networks; only random features and a one-hidden-layer NTK kernel.
Sample count is not varied as the test axis; φ is fixed.
Only random-feature (and NTK) kernel regression with a linear-equivalent teacher and Gaussian data; no other model classes.
Multiple or triple descent in total test error, and removal of the peak by optimally tuned ridge regularization: γ is not swept.

missing.what: NTK variance-component result referenced as R18 but no such row exists; fits_no_version row_ids should be empty or the row added.
Optimal ensemble-vs-bagging ratio across width and SNR (not a test of any version, but relevant context on variance sources).

record.verdict_notes: This is a theory paper; the Fig. 2 simulation dots agree with theory but no numbers are given. R8 and R15 were changed to absent because the authors state averaging eliminates the divergence. The ensemble and bagging rows were also linked to V6, since they show the peak is variance-driven. Ensembling is not regularization, so the 'optimally tuned regularization' part of V6 stays untested.

versions.untested_parts: The study analyzes random-feature regression and a single-hidden-layer NTK, not model-wise double descent in deep networks.
No sweep over training epochs or training time.
No experiment varying training sample count near the interpolation threshold to test whether more data raises test error.
The paper tests random-feature kernel regression and discusses NTK results; it does not establish the curve across all model classes.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as predicting the peak location across size, epochs, and sample count.
The paper tests whether label noise causes or exacerbates the interpolation-boundary divergence. It does not test multiple descent peaks in total test error or optimally tuned regularization.
No re-counting of complexity by an effective parameter measure to test whether the second descent becomes an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.subject: random feature kernel regression
rows.size_stated: hidden layer size n1; capacity varied by n1/m
rows.operation_detail: Analytically vary random-feature model capacity across the interpolation boundary.
rows.measure: Test error and its bias-variance decomposition as capacity varies
rows.value: The test loss diverges at the interpolation boundary; the paper identifies this as double descent, with the overparameterized regime descending again.
rows.locator: Theorem 1 and Corollary 1; Sections 3.1 and 4.2; Figure 1
rows.note: The analytic result is for random-feature kernel regression. The paper proves that bias is non-increasing with width and that the divergence comes from variance terms.
rows.check: This row rests on the theorem. Bias is finite and non-increasing (Corollary 1), and only VPX and VPXε diverge at ψ=φ. Test loss therefore spikes and then falls again. Condition SNR=100 means label noise is present.

rows.operation_detail: Evaluate test error while averaging predictions from independently initialized base learners.
rows.note: The text describes the unaveraged curve as having a peak around the interpolation threshold.
rows.check: Unaveraged baseline (kP=1); the text says the peak is around the interpolation threshold. Ridge γ=10^-6 keeps the peak finite. It duplicates R9 (same unaveraged learner).

rows.subject: random feature kernel regression
rows.size_stated: hidden layer size n1; interpolation boundary at ψ=φ
rows.operation_detail: Compare the variance decomposition with and without additive label noise.
rows.measure: Interpolation-boundary divergence in variance components and test loss
rows.value: The VPX term diverges at the interpolation boundary even without label noise.
rows.note: This shows label noise is not necessary for the divergence; the paper attributes it to interaction between sampling and initialization.
rows.check: The measure is a variance component, but VPX is part of the test loss, so the test loss diverges without label noise. The variance-driven part of V6 is observed; the label-noise-as-driver part is not needed.

rows.operation_detail: Compare the variance decomposition with and without additive label noise.
rows.measure: Interpolation-boundary divergence in variance components and test loss
rows.value: Label noise adds a divergent VPXε term and exacerbates the effect.
rows.note: The paper states that label noise amplifies but does not cause the double-descent divergence.
rows.check: Label noise adds a second divergent term, VPXε, so noise amplifies the peak. The state is observed for 'noise exacerbates', not partial.

relationships.reason: Test loss diverges at n1≈m with bounded, monotonically decreasing bias, then descends in the overparameterized regime (R1, R2, R9).
relationships.display_finding: Test loss diverged near n1=m and declined beyond interpolation, while bias remained bounded and decreased monotonically.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.reason: R1, R2 and R9 show the interpolation peak and subsequent descent in random-feature regression; Corollary 1 identifies divergent variance with bounded bias.

relationships.condition: Predictions averaged over initializations (ensembling) or over training sets (bagging)
relationships.reason: The peak shrinks as kP or kD grows and is eliminated in the infinite-average limit, so the spike depends on unaveraged single learners (R3-R8, R10-R15).
relationships.display_finding: The peak shrank as kP or kD increased and disappeared in the infinite-average limit.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Predictions averaged over initializations (ensembling) or over training sets (bagging)
source_check.reason: R3-R8 and R10-R15 show dependence on averaging: finite averaging reduces the peak, and infinite averaging removes the divergent interaction contributions.

relationships.condition: Variance as driver of the peak
relationships.reason: Only the interaction variances VPX/VPXε diverge, and removing them by ensembling or bagging removes the peak (R16, R3-R8, R10-R15). Label noise amplifies the peak (R17).
relationships.display_finding: Only the interaction variances VPX and VPXε diverged; removing them through ensembling or bagging eliminated the peak, while label noise amplified it.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Variance as driver of the peak
source_check.reason: R16-R17 identify VPX and VPXε as the divergent terms; equations (33)-(34) explain their reduction and elimination by averaging in R3-R8 and R10-R15.

relationships.reason: The peak persists with no label noise, so label noise exacerbates but is not necessary; the 'driven by label noise' reading needs qualifying (R16, R17).
relationships.display_finding: The variance-driven peak persisted without label noise and became more pronounced when label noise was added.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.reason: V6 explicitly allows variance as an alternative to label noise. R16 shows a variance-driven noiseless divergence, which supports that wording; R17 shows that label noise exacerbates it.
